draft.definition: A peptic ulcer is an open sore that develops on the inner protective lining of your stomach or the upper part of your small intestine (duodenum). Under normal conditions, a thick layer of mucus protects the stomach wall from its own harsh digestive acid and enzymes. When this protective barrier breaks down or acid levels become overwhelming, the lining erodes, leaving a raw, painful sore. In India, most peptic ulcers are caused by a bacterial infection called Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) or by regular, unmonitored use of painkiller medicines such as non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Contrary to long-held beliefs, spicy food, chilies, and everyday stress do not trigger these ulcers on their own, although they can irritate an existing sore and make the burning pain noticeably worse. With an accurate diagnosis, modern acid-suppressing tablets, and antibiotics to clear bacterial infection, most ulcers heal completely within a few weeks.

quickFacts.label: Most common cause
quickFacts.value: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) bacterial infection

quickFacts.label: Second major cause
quickFacts.value: Frequent use of NSAID painkillers (such as ibuprofen, diclofenac)

quickFacts.label: Classic symptom
quickFacts.value: Gnawing, burning pain in the upper belly between meals or at night

quickFacts.label: H. pylori prevalence in India
quickFacts.value: Up to 60% to 80% of adults carry the bacteria (often without symptoms)

quickFacts.label: Curable?
quickFacts.value: Yes, standard medical therapy heals the vast majority of ulcers

quickFacts.label: Diet role
quickFacts.value: Spicy food irritates symptoms but does not cause the ulcer

causes: Helicobacter pylori infection: This hardy bacterium survives inside stomach acid and burrows into the protective mucus layer. It causes long-standing inflammation, weakening the mucosal barrier so acid burns the delicate tissue beneath. It spreads mainly through contaminated food, unboiled water, and close household contact.

Regular use of pain medicines (NSAIDs): Common over-the-counter painkillers like ibuprofen, naproxen, and diclofenac, as well as daily aspirin, block protective chemical messengers called prostaglandins. Without prostaglandins, the stomach lining thins out, cannot produce enough mucus, and easily forms sores.

Cigarette, bidi, and gutka use: Tobacco and nicotine reduce protective bicarbonate secretion from the pancreas, cut blood flow to the stomach lining, and slow down natural tissue repair, making ulcers far more likely to bleed or recur.
Heavy alcohol consumption: Regular alcohol intake irritates the gastric mucosa, strips away mucus, and stimulates sudden acid surges.
Severe physiological stress: Life-threatening critical illness, major burns, head trauma, or extensive surgery can trigger rapid mucosal erosion ('stress ulcers') in intensive care settings.
Rare acid-producing conditions: Conditions such as Zollinger-Ellison syndrome cause rare tumours in the pancreas or duodenum that secrete massive amounts of gastrin, producing uncontrolled acid.

types.name: Duodenal ulcer
types.desc: Forms in the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine just below the stomach. Pain typically peaks 2 to 3 hours after a meal or in the middle of the night when the stomach is empty, and often feels temporarily better right after eating or taking an antacid.

types.name: Gastric ulcer
types.desc: Forms directly on the inner curve or wall of the stomach. Pain often flares up shortly after eating food because the stomach releases digestive acid to break down the meal, sometimes leading to early fullness, nausea, and reduced appetite.

types.name: Esophageal ulcer
types.desc: Occurs at the lower end of the food pipe (esophagus), often related to chronic, severe acid reflux (GERD) or prolonged pill-induced irritation.

diagnosis: Doctors take a detailed history of your upper belly pain, food triggers, and exact list of painkiller tablets, blood thinners, and joint supplements.
Testing for H. pylori infection is standard and can be done via a simple urea breath test, a stool antigen test, or during an endoscopy.

An upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy (gastroscopy) is the gold standard investigation. A doctor inserts a thin, flexible tube with a camera down your throat to look directly at the stomach and duodenum, measure ulcer size, and take small tissue samples (biopsies).
Barium swallow or upper GI X-ray series is occasionally used when endoscopy is not immediately available, though it cannot provide tissue biopsies.

investigations.purpose: Directly visualises the ulcer, checks for bleeding, and allows biopsy for H. pylori or abnormal cells
Measures haemoglobin to detect hidden slow bleeding and anaemia caused by the ulcer
Checks total body iron stores if chronic microscopic blood loss is suspected

investigations.test: Urea Breath Test or Stool Antigen Test
investigations.purpose: Non-invasive test to confirm active H. pylori infection or verify its clearance after treatment
Rules out gallstones, gallbladder inflammation, or liver conditions that cause similar upper belly pain
Ensures healthy kidney function before choosing specific antibiotics or ulcer medications

modernTreatment: Antibiotic combination therapy: If H. pylori is found, your doctor prescribes a targeted 14-day course combining two or three antibiotics with an acid reducer. Finishing every tablet exactly as prescribed is essential to eradicate the bacteria and prevent treatment failure.

Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs): Powerful acid suppressors like pantoprazole or omeprazole block the acid-producing pumps in stomach cells, lowering stomach acidity so the raw ulcer bed can heal quickly.
H2-receptor blockers: Medicines such as famotidine reduce acid production and provide an alternative or night-time support as advised by your doctor.
Mucosal protectants: Liquid coatings containing sucralfate form a physical barrier over the ulcer crater, shielding it from direct acid, bile, and digestive enzymes.
Stopping harmful painkillers: Your doctor will immediately review and stop unnecessary NSAIDs, switching you to safer pain relief options such as paracetamol when needed.
Emergency endoscopic therapy: If an ulcer bleeds heavily, doctors treat it directly during an emergency endoscopy using heat probes, clips, or adrenaline injections to seal the ruptured vessel.
ayurvedaView: Ayurvedic texts describe chronic burning abdominal pain and acid conditions under terms like Parinama Shula and Annadrava Shula, closely linked to aggravated Pitta dosha combined with Vata.
Excess Pitta is viewed as an overload of heat, sharp quality (tikshna), and sourness (amla) that irritates the stomach tissue, while Vata imbalance can impair digestive rhythm.
Traditional regimens focus on Pitta-pacifying (cooling, soothing) foods, mindful meal timing, and cooling herbs to support digestive comfort alongside medical care.
Ayurvedic herbs should never replace modern antibiotics for H. pylori or replace prescribed acid-reducing drugs, as untreated ulcers carry a risk of perforation or severe bleeding.

herbsUsed.name: Licorice (Yashtimadhu)
herbsUsed.note: Traditionally used to soothe the gut lining. Deglycyrrhizinated forms support the stomach mucus layer, but whole licorice must be avoided in people with high blood pressure without doctor review.

herbsUsed.name: Amla (Indian Gooseberry)
herbsUsed.note: Known in traditional systems for digestive balance; however, its natural sour acidity can sometimes aggravate active gastric sores in sensitive individuals.

herbsUsed.name: Shatavari
herbsUsed.note: Considered soothing and cooling in Ayurveda to support gut comfort, though rigorous human trials for ulcer healing remain limited.

herbsUsed.name: Turmeric
herbsUsed.note: Curcumin possesses anti-inflammatory properties, but concentrated extracts may cause stomach upset and should only be used as mild kitchen spice during active ulceration.

nutrition: Eat regular, moderate meals instead of fasting for long hours or consuming huge, heavy dinners that overfill the stomach and trigger heavy acid production.
Include soft, easily digestible Indian foods such as moong dal khichdi, soft rice, boiled oats, vegetable soups, and lightly cooked bottle gourd (lauki) or ridge gourd (torai).
Fresh, room-temperature curd (dahi) or mild buttermilk (chaas) without heavy green chilies can provide natural probiotics that soothe the digestive tract, especially during antibiotic therapy.
Cut down on heavily fried snacks like samosas, pakoras, puri, bhujia, and rich oily gravies, which delay stomach emptying and trigger excess acid wash.
Minimise red chili powder, raw green chilies, black pepper, and excessive garam masala while the ulcer is actively healing, as they irritate the raw tissue.
Avoid citrus juices, raw onions, and vinegar on an empty stomach if they trigger sharp burning pain.
Strictly avoid alcohol, energy drinks, and strong black tea or filter coffee, as both caffeine and alcohol stimulate stomach acid and erode the lining.
lifestyle: Stop all forms of tobacco completely, including cigarettes, bidis, gutka, and khaini. Smoking directly delays ulcer healing and doubles the risk of repeat ulcers.
Do not lie down immediately after eating. Stay upright for at least 2 to 3 hours after dinner to let your stomach empty smoothly.
Elevate the head of your bed by 6 to 8 inches if you experience nighttime burning or acid reflux along with your ulcer.
Maintain consistent meal timings every day so your digestive system is not subjected to long stretches of high-acid fasting.
Practice structured stress-reduction techniques such as daily outdoor walking, deep breathing, or light reading, as mental distress lowers gut mucosal blood flow.
Stay adequately hydrated throughout the day by sipping clean, boiled or filtered water, avoiding large gulps right in the middle of heavy meals.
yogaActivity: Practice gentle breathing exercises like Anulom Vilom (alternate nostril breathing) and Sheetali or Sheetkari pranayama to cool and calm the autonomic nervous system.
Incorporate relaxing, resting postures such as Shavasana, Supta Baddha Konasana with bolster support, and gentle Vajrasana for 10 minutes after light meals.
Avoid strenuous abdominal core exercises, heavy crunches, forceful forward bends, and vigorous Kapalbhati while an ulcer is actively inflamed or painful.
Skip heavy weightlifting, intense isometric straining, or holding your breath (Valsalva manoeuvre) under heavy gym barbells until your doctor confirms the ulcer has completely healed.
homeopathyNote: There is no reliable scientific or clinical evidence showing that homeopathic products can clear H. pylori infection or heal an open peptic ulcer.
Relying solely on homeopathy for peptic ulcer disease carries serious risks, including silent internal bleeding, sudden perforation, and stomach wall scarring.
Always follow your physician's prescribed diagnostic plan and modern medications.
evidenceNotes: Strong evidence: Eradicating H. pylori with antibiotic regimens and using proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) heals over 85% to 90% of peptic ulcers and prevents life-threatening recurrence.
Strong evidence: Stopping non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) allows the natural gastric mucus layer to regenerate and prevents recurrent mucosal bleeding.
Moderate evidence: Quitting smoking significantly speeds up ulcer healing rates and cuts relapse rates across clinical trials.

Limited or weak evidence: Herbal remedies and traditional powders show mixed or weak clinical evidence for independently closing ulcer craters. No herb, diet or product can make it go away without treating the root cause.
shouldNotDo: Do not self-prescribe over-the-counter pain relievers such as brufen, combiflam, voveran, or aspirin whenever you have a headache, backache, or fever; talk to your doctor about safer choices.
Do not stop your prescribed antibiotics midway just because the stomach pain vanished in three days. Incomplete antibiotic courses cause resistant H. pylori that is much harder to treat.
Do not consume milk by the litre thinking it 'coats' the stomach. While cold milk feels soothing for a few minutes, milk proteins and calcium trigger a strong 'acid rebound' an hour later.
Do not ignore recurring black, sticky stools, assuming they are just caused by food, indigestion, or routine constipation.
Do not skip meals or follow extreme dry fasting routines while recovering from an active peptic ulcer.
medicationSafety: Take proton pump inhibitors (like pantoprazole or omeprazole) exactly as advised by your doctor, usually 30 to 60 minutes before your first meal of the day for best acid control.
If your doctor prescribes an antibiotic kit for H. pylori, complete all tablets for the entire 14-day duration without skipping doses.
Inform your physician if you take blood thinners (like aspirin, clopidogrel, or warfarin), as these greatly raise the danger of ulcer bleeding and require protective acid-suppressing cover.
Do not take antacid liquids and sucralfate at the exact same minute as other tablets, as they can block the absorption of your blood pressure or thyroid medicines; leave at least a 2-hour gap.
complications: Internal bleeding: An ulcer can slowly eat into a stomach blood vessel, causing chronic fatigue and anaemia, or break into a major artery causing massive, life-threatening blood vomiting.

Gastric perforation: The ulcer burns a hole completely through the wall of the stomach or duodenum, leaking digestive contents into the sterile abdominal cavity (peritonitis), requiring immediate emergency surgery.

Gastric outlet obstruction: Chronic ulcers near the pyloric channel cause severe swelling and dense scar tissue, blocking food from passing into the intestines and causing persistent projectile vomiting.
Stomach cancer risk: Long-term, untreated H. pylori infection causing chronic atrophic gastritis is an established risk factor for certain forms of gastric cancer.
emergencySigns: Vomiting fresh bright red blood or dark brown material that looks like wet coffee grounds
Passing loose, sticky, foul-smelling, jet-black stools (known as melaena)
Sudden, excruciating, sharp pain in your belly that spreads quickly and makes your abdomen feel rigid or hard as a wooden board
Feeling suddenly faint, dizzy, unusually pale, or losing consciousness
Inability to keep any liquids down accompanied by continuous vomiting and high fever
whenToSeeDoctor: You have persistent, gnawing, or burning pain in your upper abdomen that lasts more than two weeks
You find yourself regularly taking antacid gels or over-the-counter acid-blockers just to get through the day
You feel full unusually fast after eating only a few bites of food, or have unexplained weight loss
You experience unexplained weakness, breathlessness while climbing stairs, and unusual paleness
You need long-term daily painkillers for joint pain or arthritis and experience stomach discomfort

faqs.q: Does eating very spicy Indian food cause a peptic ulcer?
faqs.a: No. Modern medical science proves that spicy food, chilies, and oily curries do not cause ulcers on their own. The true primary causes are H. pylori bacteria and NSAID painkiller medications. However, if an ulcer is already open and raw, strong chilies and spices will sting the tissue and worsen your burning pain.

faqs.q: Can drinking cold milk heal my stomach ulcer?
faqs.a: No. Cold milk can provide a brief soothing sensation because it temporarily buffers stomach acid. However, milk stimulates your stomach to produce even more acid and digestive enzymes an hour later (known as acid rebound), which can aggravate the ulcer. Rely on prescribed medicines rather than milk therapy.

faqs.q: How long does it take for a peptic ulcer to heal?
faqs.a: With regular use of prescribed acid-suppressing tablets (like PPIs) and eradication of H. pylori with antibiotics, most uncomplicated duodenal ulcers heal in 4 weeks, and gastric ulcers generally heal within 6 to 8 weeks.

faqs.q: Which painkiller is safe to take if I have a history of ulcers?
faqs.a: Paracetamol is generally considered much safer for the stomach lining than NSAIDs like ibuprofen, diclofenac, or naproxen. However, you should always consult your doctor to confirm what pain medication and dose is safe for your specific health history.

faqs.q: Can stress alone give me a stomach ulcer?
faqs.a: Everyday emotional or workplace stress does not directly cause a peptic ulcer by itself, though it can worsen your symptoms and lead to unhealthy habits like smoking, skipping meals, or excess tea. Only severe physiological trauma—such as major burns or intensive care illness—causes true stress-related gastric ulcers.

peripheral-artery-disease.name: Peripheral Artery Disease

draft.definition: Peripheral Artery Disease (PAD) is a circulatory condition where narrowed arteries reduce blood flow to your limbs, most commonly the legs and feet. This narrowing occurs due to atherosclerosis, a gradual buildup of fatty deposits called plaque on the artery walls. Because muscles do not receive enough oxygen-rich blood during exertion, a classic cramp-like muscle ache during walking (called intermittent claudication) often develops. In India, PAD is increasingly common due to high rates of diabetes, smoking, bidi use, and uncontrolled lipid levels. Many people dismiss leg pain as normal aging or simple joint pain, leaving this serious sign of widespread cardiovascular disease undetected until significant complications occur.

quickFacts.label: Primary cause
quickFacts.value: Atherosclerosis (fatty plaque buildup in leg arteries)

quickFacts.label: Classic symptom
quickFacts.value: Leg muscle cramps during walking that ease with rest (claudication)

quickFacts.label: Major risk factors in India
quickFacts.value: Type 2 diabetes, smoking, bidi, high blood pressure, and abnormal cholesterol

quickFacts.label: Key screening test
quickFacts.value: Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI) comparing arm and ankle blood pressures

quickFacts.label: Global prevalence
quickFacts.value: Over 200 million people worldwide (WHO / Lancet)

quickFacts.label: Core danger
quickFacts.value: Significantly raised risk of heart attack, stroke, non-healing ulcers, or amputation

causes: Atherosclerosis: Plaque made of cholesterol, calcium, and cellular waste accumulates on the inner lining of peripheral arteries, gradually narrowing the blood vessel lumen.
Smoking and smokeless tobacco: Tobacco in any form, including cigarettes, bidi, gutka, and khaini, damages vessel linings, raises inflammation, and markedly accelerates artery blockages.
Type 2 diabetes: High blood sugar damages blood vessel walls and nerves, making Indian adults with diabetes particularly prone to severe and early-onset peripheral blockages.
High cholesterol and dyslipidemia: High LDL cholesterol and raised triglycerides contribute directly to the fatty plaque that clogs arteries.
High blood pressure: Constant pressure strains arterial walls, creating micro-tears where fatty plaques lodge and grow.
Advanced age: Arteries stiffen and plaque burdens naturally increase after age 50, especially in those with metabolic risk factors.
Chronic kidney disease: Impaired kidney function changes mineral balance and accelerates arterial calcification.

types.name: Asymptomatic PAD
types.desc: Blood flow is reduced, but the person feels no symptoms, often because they walk very little or have diabetic nerve damage masking the pain.

types.name: Intermittent Claudication
types.desc: Predictable muscle pain, cramping, or fatigue in the calf, thigh, or buttock triggered by walking a specific distance and relieved within minutes of standing still.

types.name: Critical Limb Ischemia (CLI)
types.desc: A severe, advanced stage where blood flow is so low that severe pain persists even while resting or lying down, often accompanied by non-healing sores or gangrene.

types.name: Acute Limb Ischemia
types.desc: A sudden, emergency blockage caused by a blood clot or dislodged embolus, leading to rapid onset of coldness, pain, pale skin, and loss of pulse in the leg.

diagnosis: Careful physical examination: The doctor checks pulses in the groin, behind the knees, over the ankles, and on top of the feet, and looks for cool skin, hair loss, or color changes.
Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI): A quick, painless test comparing blood pressure in your ankle to blood pressure in your arm using a Doppler probe. A value of 0.90 or lower confirms PAD.
Treadmill test for ABI: Checking ABI immediately after walking on a treadmill helps detect narrowed vessels when resting values look borderline.
Duplex ultrasound: High-frequency sound waves visualize blood flow and pinpoint specific narrowed or blocked sections in the leg arteries.
CT angiography (CTA) or MR angiography (MRA): Detailed imaging used when surgical repair or stenting is being planned.

investigations.purpose: Primary non-invasive test to confirm peripheral arterial narrowing
Evaluates average blood sugar control over the last three months
Detects underlying diabetes or prediabetes
Measures total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and triglycerides to guide lipid-lowering therapy
Assesses kidney health before planning contrast scans or adjusting medications
Rules out anemia or underlying infection if foot sores are present
Assesses systemic vascular inflammation

modernTreatment: Supervised exercise therapy: A structured walk-rest-walk program is the gold-standard initial treatment, stimulating the growth of small collateral vessels to bypass blockages.
Antiplatelet medications: Doctors prescribe medicines such as aspirin or clopidogrel to reduce the risk of blood clots, heart attack, and stroke.
Lipid-lowering therapy: High-intensity statins (such as atorvastatin) are prescribed to stabilize plaque and lower LDL cholesterol to strict target levels.
Blood pressure and diabetes control: Managing blood pressure (often with ARBs like losartan or calcium channel blockers like amlodipine) and keeping blood sugar well managed protects blood vessels.
Symptom-relief medications: Specific medicines like cilostazol may be prescribed as advised by your doctor to improve pain-free walking distance.
Endovascular procedures: Angioplasty with or without stenting uses a small balloon and mesh tube inserted through a puncture to widen narrowed vessels.
Surgical bypass: In complex or extensive blockages, a vascular surgeon redirects blood flow around the blocked segment using a healthy vein or synthetic graft.
ayurvedaView: Ayurvedic classical texts do not define PAD as a single modern entity. It is conceptually understood as an imbalance involving Vata dosha along with Kapha and Meda (fatty tissue), creating obstruction (Avarana) in the blood channels (Raktavaha Srotas).
Traditional guidance emphasizes clearing channel obstruction through light, easily digestible food (Langhana), warming spices, and disciplined physical movement.
Ayurvedic therapies such as gentle warm herbalized oil application must be approached with extreme caution, as vigorous massage or hot fomentation can damage delicate, ischemic skin.
Ayurvedic formulations may offer general metabolic and digestive support alongside care, but no herb, diet, or product can make structural artery blockages go away.

herbsUsed.name: Garlic
herbsUsed.note: Traditional culinary herb shown in small clinical trials to have modest effects on lipid levels and platelet aggregation. Use standard food amounts; avoid high-dose supplements without medical advice because they can increase bleeding risk when taken alongside blood thinners.

herbsUsed.name: Turmeric
herbsUsed.note: Contains curcumin, which possesses antioxidant and mild anti-inflammatory properties in laboratory models. Clinical evidence in human arterial disease remains limited, and it cannot replace prescribed vascular medicines.

herbsUsed.name: Arjuna
herbsUsed.note: Traditionally used in Indian systems for cardiovascular support. Robust clinical trials demonstrating improvement in walking distance or arterial patency in PAD are lacking.

herbsUsed.name: Ginger
herbsUsed.note: A warming spice with mild circulatory stimulation properties in traditional use, but no human trials show it opens narrowed leg arteries.

nutrition: Adopt a heart-healthy diet aligned with ICMR-NIN dietary guidelines: build meals around whole grains, seasonal vegetables, pulses, and healthy nuts.

Cut down on saturated fats and avoid trans fats entirely; replace vanaspati, palm oil, and deep-fried snacks (such as samosas, pakoras, and bhujia) with moderate amounts of cold-pressed mustard, groundnut, or sesame oil.
Keep total salt intake under 5 grams per day (about one level teaspoon), watching out for hidden sodium in pickles, papads, chutneys, and packaged mixtures.
Include fiber-rich foods daily: oats, barley, whole moong, chana, methi leaves, and guava help manage both cholesterol and blood glucose levels.
Avoid refined carbohydrates, sugary drinks, sweets, and bakery goods that raise triglycerides and worsen insulin resistance.
Stay adequately hydrated with plain water, buttermilk, or clear vegetable soups to prevent sluggish blood flow.
lifestyle: Quit all forms of tobacco immediately. Smoking, bidi, and chewing gutka are the single most destructive factors in PAD; quitting stops the rapid progression of blockages.

Engage in structured walking therapy: walk until leg discomfort reaches moderate intensity, stop and rest until pain completely subsides, and then walk again, aiming for 30 to 45 minutes total, 3 to 5 times weekly.
Inspect both feet daily: check toes, heels, and soles for red marks, cuts, blisters, cracks, or fungal patches using a hand mirror or assistance from family.
Wear clean, seamless cotton socks and properly fitted, supportive footwear; never walk barefoot, even inside the home or at places of worship.
Keep feet clean and dry, especially between the toes, and apply a gentle moisturizer to heels and soles to prevent cracks, avoiding the spaces between toes.
Never apply direct hot water bottles, heating pads, or very hot water to your feet, as reduced sensation can lead to severe burns without warning.
yogaActivity: Gentle foot and ankle movements: simple seated ankle rotations, toe flexing, and ankle pumps (Sukshma Vyayama) stimulate local microcirculation without excessive strain.

Supported poses: Gentle asanas like Tadasana (Mountain Pose), Dandasana, and supported Viparita Karani (legs resting gently against a wall with a cushion under the hips) can help promote venous and arterial tone if cleared by your doctor.
Controlled breathing: Slow, relaxing pranayama practices such as Anulom Vilom and Bhramari help reduce sympathetic nervous stress and support healthy blood pressure.

Avoid strenuous poses: Do not perform aggressive inverted poses, intense hot yoga, or fast, forceful breathing exercises like rapid Kapalabhati if severe arterial disease or high blood pressure is present.
homeopathyNote: There is no reliable scientific evidence demonstrating that homeopathic remedies can clear narrowed arteries, improve walking distance, or prevent gangrene in PAD.
Relying solely on alternative therapies while delaying proven cardiovascular treatments increases the risk of limb loss and major heart events.
Any complementary approach must never replace prescribed blood-thinning, statin, or surgical therapies recommended by a qualified vascular specialist.
evidenceNotes: Strong evidence: Supervised exercise therapy, smoking cessation, high-intensity statin therapy, and antiplatelet drugs significantly reduce cardiovascular death, improve walking distance, and lower amputation rates.
Strong evidence: Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI) is an accurate, highly reproducible non-invasive screening tool for identifying lower extremity arterial narrowing.
Moderate evidence: Endovascular revascularization (angioplasty and stenting) provides reliable symptom relief and ulcer healing in appropriately selected anatomical lesions.
Weak or no evidence: Herbal extracts, dietary supplements, foot-massage devices, and magnet therapy lack robust clinical proof for clearing arterial plaque or restoring leg blood flow.
shouldNotDo: Do not ignore recurring leg cramps during walking by assuming they are just a sign of getting older, calcium deficiency, or ordinary arthritis.
Do not walk barefoot on hot floors, temple tiles, coarse gravel, or rough outdoor surfaces.
Do not use hot water bags, electric heating pads, or intense hot water soaks on your feet to warm them up.
Do not cut your own corns, calluses, or ingrown toenails with scissors, blades, or nail cutters; have a trained foot-care professional or doctor manage them.
Do not stop or skip prescribed statins, blood thinners, or blood pressure medicines simply because leg discomfort improves.
Do not purchase unproven tonics, herbal blood cleansers, or magnetic wraps claiming to dissolve artery blockages.
medicationSafety: Take antiplatelet medicines (like aspirin or clopidogrel) exactly as advised by your doctor; inform your dentist or surgeon before any planned procedure.
If taking statins (such as atorvastatin), notify your doctor if you develop unexplained muscle pain, severe tenderness, or unusually dark urine.
Never combine over-the-counter painkillers (such as ibuprofen or diclofenac) with blood-thinning medicines without medical approval, as this sharply raises stomach bleeding risks.
Store all medicines in their original labeled packaging away from moisture and heat.
If prescribed cilostazol for claudication, take it as directed; report any unusual heart pounding, headaches, or fluid swelling to your doctor promptly.
complications: Critical limb ischemia: Severe continuous pain in the toes and feet even when resting, keeping you awake at night.
Non-healing foot ulcers: Minor sores, scrapes, or blisters that fail to heal due to lack of blood supply, frequently turning infected.
Gangrene: Death of tissue in toes or the foot due to complete loss of blood flow, appearing black, shriveled, or draining foul-smelling fluid.
Limb amputation: Partial or complete amputation of toes, foot, or lower leg to prevent life-threatening systemic infection.
Heart attack and stroke: PAD indicates widespread systemic atherosclerosis, dramatically raising the risk of life-threatening events in the heart and brain.
emergencySigns: Sudden, severe leg or foot pain accompanied by a pale, cold, bluish, or numb limb: suspected acute arterial occlusion requiring emergency hospital care within hours
A rapidly spreading black, purple, or foul-smelling discoloration on any toe or part of the foot (gangrene)
A foot sore that develops spreading redness, red streaks moving up the leg, fever, chills, or severe swelling
Crushing chest pressure, pain spreading to the arm or jaw, sudden shortness of breath, or sudden weakness/numbness on one side of the body
whenToSeeDoctor: You get cramping, heaviness, or pain in your calves, thighs, or hips when walking that resolves after a few minutes of rest.
Your feet or lower legs feel consistently colder than the rest of your body, or appear pale when elevated.
You notice a cut, blister, scratch, or sore on your foot or toe that does not heal after 7 to 10 days.
You have diabetes, a history of smoking, or high cholesterol and are aged 50 or older, even if you feel no obvious leg pain.
You notice sudden thinning of leg skin, loss of leg hair, or unusually slow-growing, thickened toenails.

faqs.q: How does peripheral artery disease differ from varicose veins?
faqs.a: They affect different blood vessels. Peripheral artery disease involves narrowed arteries that struggle to carry oxygen-rich blood down into the legs, causing pain during walking. Varicose veins involve weakened valves in veins that struggle to return blood up toward the heart, leading to swollen, twisted veins and heaviness after prolonged standing.

faqs.q: Can walking really help if walking is what brings on the pain?
faqs.a: Yes. Supervised walking is the most effective lifestyle therapy for PAD. Walking until pain starts, resting until it clears, and repeating this cycle trains your leg muscles to use oxygen more efficiently and encourages tiny collateral vessels to open around the blockages.

faqs.q: Does having PAD mean I am at risk of a heart attack?
faqs.a: Yes. Atherosclerosis is rarely confined to one limb. If plaque has narrowed the arteries in your legs, there is a strong possibility that similar plaque exists in the arteries supplying your heart and brain, making overall cardiovascular management vital.

faqs.q: Can herbs or oils melt away the blockages in my leg arteries?
faqs.a: No. Plaque is a calcified, fibrous buildup within the artery wall. No herb, diet, massage oil, or product can make it go away. Effective care relies on evidence-based lifestyle changes, medications, and when needed, angioplasty or surgical bypass.

faqs.q: Why are diabetic individuals at higher risk for severe PAD?
faqs.a: Diabetes damages the lining of blood vessels and accelerates plaque formation. Furthermore, diabetic nerve damage (neuropathy) often blunts pain perception, meaning individuals may not feel the warning ache of claudication until severe ulcers or gangrene have already formed.

pigmentation.name: Pigmentation & Melasma
notes: 1 reference(s) from untrusted sites dropped

draft.definition: Pigmentation refers to the natural colouring of your skin, driven by a brown-black pigment called melanin. Melanin is produced by specialized cells named melanocytes to protect your skin from harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation. When melanocytes become overactive, they produce excess melanin in patches, leading to hyperpigmentation. In India, where most individuals have Fitzpatrick skin phototypes III to V, hyperpigmentation is one of the most common reasons people visit a skin doctor. Melasma is a specific, chronic form of hyperpigmentation that presents as symmetrical, brownish or slate-grey patches, most frequently across the cheeks, forehead, bridge of the nose, chin, and upper lip. While hyperpigmentation and melasma are medically harmless in terms of physical pain or organ damage, they can be persistent, recurrent, and emotionally distressing. Sun exposure, intense heat, hormonal changes during pregnancy or oral contraceptive use, thyroid dysfunction, and skin inflammation from acne or aggressive parlour treatments are major triggers for Indian skin.

quickFacts.label: What it is
quickFacts.value: Excess melanin production causing darker patches on the skin

quickFacts.label: Most common sites
quickFacts.value: Cheeks, forehead, upper lip, chin, and bridge of the nose

quickFacts.label: Key triggers
quickFacts.value: Sunlight (UV and visible light), heat, hormones, and skin injury

quickFacts.label: Hormonal link
quickFacts.value: Common in pregnancy (chloasma), PCOS, and thyroid disorders

quickFacts.label: Skin type impact
quickFacts.value: Deeper Indian skin tones (types III-V) produce pigment quickly after irritation

quickFacts.label: Treatment timeline
quickFacts.value: Slow and gradual, taking several months of consistent care

causes: Ultraviolet (UV) radiation and visible blue light: Sunlight activates melanocytes to churn out excess melanin. In India, year-round intense UV index and exposure to visible light from strong overhead sun make sun protection essential.

Hormonal shifts: High levels of estrogen and progesterone sensitize melanocytes. This explains why melasma frequently flares during pregnancy, hormone replacement therapy, or while taking oral contraceptive pills.

Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH): Any skin injury, severe acne breakout, eczema patch, insect bite, chemical burn, or aggressive facial treatment can leave a dark mark once healed, especially in brown skin.
Endocrine and metabolic disorders: Thyroid imbalances (hypothyroidism) and insulin resistance often travel with altered skin pigmentation or conditions like acanthosis nigricans and melasma.

Unregulated cosmetic and bleaching creams: Frequent use of over-the-counter creams containing hidden potent steroids (such as clobetasol), hydroquinone, or heavy metals damages the skin barrier and triggers rebound hyperpigmentation or steroid-induced rosacea.

Heat exposure (infrared radiation): Working near hot gas stoves, tandoors, furnaces, or exercising in unventilated, high-heat environments stimulates dermal blood vessels and triggers melanocytes even without direct sun.
Genetic predisposition: Having a family member with melasma or marked hyperpigmentation significantly increases personal risk.

types.name: Epidermal Melasma
types.desc: The excess melanin sits in the top superficial layer of the skin (epidermis). It appears light brown with well-defined borders and responds most readily to medical creams and sun protection.

types.name: Dermal Melasma
types.desc: Pigment deposits sink deeper into the dermis. It often looks bluish-grey or slate-brown with ill-defined borders and is notoriously stubborn, requiring long-term care and gentle medical guidance.

types.name: Mixed Melasma
types.desc: The most common form seen in Indian clinics. Pigment is present in both superficial and deep skin layers, appearing as uneven dark brown or greyish patches.

types.name: Post-Inflammatory Hyperpigmentation (PIH)
types.desc: Flat dark spots left behind after acne, burns, waxing irritation, or skin rashes heal. The colour ranges from pinkish-brown to dark black depending on depth.

types.name: Acanthosis Nigricans
types.desc: Velvety, thickened, dark skin folds usually found around the neck, armpits, and groin, strongly linked with insulin resistance, obesity, and metabolic conditions.

diagnosis: Clinical examination by a qualified dermatologist: A visual inspection of the face, neck, and hands under natural lighting to evaluate the distribution and pattern of pigmentation.
Wood's lamp examination: A handheld ultraviolet light used in a darkened room to identify whether the pigment is superficial (epidermal) or deep (dermal), which helps guide treatment choices.
Dermoscopy: A specialized non-invasive skin surface microscope that examines pigment networks, vascular changes, and rules out signs of steroid damage or exogenous ochronosis.
Medical history review: Doctors will check for pregnancy, oral contraceptive usage, cosmetic applications, family history, and systemic symptoms like weight fluctuations or menstrual irregularity.
Skin biopsy (rare): Occasionally performed only if a doctor needs to rule out other skin conditions such as lichen planus pigmentosus, fixed drug eruptions, or rare melanocytic lesions.

investigations.purpose: Identifies underlying thyroid dysfunction, which is frequently associated with recalcitrant melasma
Evaluates active thyroid hormone levels alongside TSH when thyroid disease is suspected
Screens for prediabetes or diabetes, particularly when velvety darkening is present on the neck or armpits
Measures average blood sugar over the past three months to detect insulin resistance
Rules out underlying nutritional deficiencies or systemic illness that can influence skin tone and health
Evaluates body iron stores, as both iron overload and severe deficiencies can present with skin changes

modernTreatment: Broad-spectrum photoprotection: Daily application of broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 to 50+ and high UVA protection (PA+++ or PA++++). Tinted sunscreens containing iron oxides are especially helpful because they block visible light that triggers melasma.

Topical depigmenting agents: First-line medical creams prescribed by dermatologists include azelaic acid, kojic acid, tranexamic acid, glycolic acid, niacinamide, and carefully supervised hydroquinone courses.

Triple combination creams: A medically formulated cream containing hydroquinone, a mild steroid, and tretinoin is effective for short-term control. It must be used strictly under a doctor's supervision for limited weeks to prevent severe skin thinning and rebound darkening.
Oral medications: In resistant cases, dermatologists may prescribe low-dose oral tranexamic acid after screening for blood clotting risks. It reduces vascular triggers and melanocyte activity.

In-clinic chemical peels: Superficial peels using glycolic acid, lactic acid, or salicylic acid carried out by trained professionals can gently remove outer pigment. Deep aggressive peels are avoided in brown skin due to high risk of PIH.

Laser and light therapies: Low-fluence Q-switched lasers or picosecond lasers may be used cautiously in selected stubborn cases, but improper laser use can significantly worsen pigmentation in Indian skin.
ayurvedaView: In classical Ayurveda, facial pigmentation and discolouration are closely related to conditions like Vyanga and Neelika, described as painless, dark circular spots on the face.
It is traditionally viewed as an aggravation of Pitta dosha (specifically Bhrajaka Pitta, which governs skin lustre and temperature) interacting with vitiated Vata and Rakta dhatu (blood tissue).

Factors said to aggravate Pitta and Rakta include excessive intake of pungent, sour, and salty foods (katu, amla, lavana), prolonged exposure to direct sun and heat, chronic anger, and irregular digestion.
Ayurvedic care focuses on soothing internal heat, improving digestion, gentle external pastes (lepa), and cooling lifestyle practices alongside modern medical management.

Traditional remedies should be viewed as supportive care. Potent kitchen pastes like raw lime juice, baking soda, or raw garlic must never be applied to the skin, as they cause severe contact dermatitis and deepen pigmentation.

herbsUsed.name: Licorice (Yashtimadhu)
herbsUsed.note: Contains glabridin, which has been shown in laboratory studies to inhibit tyrosinase, the enzyme that produces melanin. Often used in supportive topical formulations.

herbsUsed.name: Turmeric (Haridra)
herbsUsed.note: Curcumin provides natural antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, but raw kitchen turmeric paste can stain or irritate sensitive facial skin.

herbsUsed.name: Amla (Amalaki)
herbsUsed.note: Rich in natural vitamin C and polyphenols that help fight cellular oxidative stress when consumed as part of a balanced diet.

herbsUsed.name: Neem
herbsUsed.note: Traditionally valued for soothing inflamed, acne-prone skin, which helps lower the chance of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.

nutrition: Eat a diet rich in diverse antioxidants: Include seasonal Indian fruits like amla, guava, papaya, oranges, pomegranate, and watermelons to combat free-radical damage from sunlight.

Consume plenty of fresh vegetables: Incorporate colourful vegetables such as carrots, tomatoes, spinach, methi, beetroot, and bell peppers. Cooked tomatoes provide lycopene, which supports skin resilience.
Ensure adequate micronutrients: Zinc, vitamin C, vitamin E, and selenium support skin barrier repair. Include soaked almonds, walnuts, pumpkin seeds, and sunflower seeds daily.
Stay hydrated: Drink 2 to 3 litres of clean water throughout the day. Hydration keeps the skin supple and improves natural skin turnover.

Minimize refined sugars and ultra-processed foods: High glycemic Indian snacks like mithai, refined flour puris, samosas, and sugary drinks trigger insulin spikes that worsen hormonal imbalances and acanthosis nigricans.
Incorporate gentle cooling spices: Use coriander, cumin, fennel, and modest amounts of turmeric in cooking while limiting extremely fiery red chilli pastes and rancid oils.
lifestyle: Strict daily sun protection: Apply a broad-spectrum sunscreen 15 to 20 minutes before stepping out, even on cloudy days, and reapply every 2 to 3 hours if sweating or outdoors.
Use physical barriers: Wear a broad-brimmed hat, carry an umbrella, or use a clean cotton scarf (dupatta) to shield your face when moving around in the afternoon sun.
Avoid heat exposure where possible: Stand away from direct steam while cooking, allow the kitchen to stay well-ventilated, and avoid washing your face with excessively hot water.
Gentle skincare routine: Switch to a mild, fragrance-free cleanser and a soothing ceramide-based moisturizer. Never scrub the face with coarse walnut scrubs or loofahs.
Manage daily stress: High cortisol levels can stimulate hormonal pathways that worsen melasma. Prioritize 7 to 8 hours of restful sleep every night.
yogaActivity: Pranayama for stress reduction: Gentle breathing practices like Anulom Vilom (alternate nostril breathing), Sheetali, and Bhramari help calm the nervous system and manage stress-induced hormonal flares.

Avoid vigorous inverted poses during active heat: While gentle yoga is beneficial, avoid prolonged headstands (Sirsasana) or hot yoga rooms if you notice facial flushing, as vascular dilation can worsen melasma.
Restorative asanas: Incorporate calming postures like Balasana (Child's Pose), Supta Baddha Konasana (Reclining Bound Angle Pose), and Shavasana (Corpse Pose) to promote relaxation and restful sleep.
Outdoor exercise timing: If you practice yoga, run, or walk outdoors, schedule your sessions early in the morning before 8:00 AM or in the evening after sunset to avoid peak UV hours.
homeopathyNote: There is no reliable scientific evidence demonstrating that homeopathic medicines can cure melasma, regulate melanocyte activity, or remove deep pigmentation.
People seeking homeopathic treatment must not abandon evidence-based sun protection measures or dermatological care.
Avoid unlabelled liquid preparations or over-the-counter drop mixtures that make unproven claims to wipe away pigmentation.
evidenceNotes: Strong evidence: Daily use of broad-spectrum sunscreens (especially tinted formulas containing iron oxide) and topical agents like azelaic acid, tranexamic acid, and short-term triple combination creams consistently lighten melasma.
Strong evidence: Oral tranexamic acid prescribed by a dermatologist shows solid efficacy in treating stubborn, recurrent melasma in clinical trials.
Moderate evidence: Superficial chemical peels (such as glycolic and salicylic acid) and topical licorice extracts provide supportive lightening when combined with sun protection.
Weak or limited evidence: Dietary herbal supplements, home face packs, and standalone laser treatments without sun protection have weak or inconsistent evidence and carry a risk of rebound darkening.
shouldNotDo: Do not buy over-the-counter 'fairness' or 'triple action' steroid creams from local pharmacies without a prescription. These often contain strong steroids like clobetasol, which thin the skin, cause permanent red veins, and lead to terrible rebound pigmentation.

Do not apply harsh home remedies such as lemon juice, raw apple cider vinegar, baking soda, or undiluted garlic to your face. These cause chemical burns, severe irritation, and deep post-inflammatory marks.
Do not rub, scrub, or exfoliate pigmented patches aggressively. Friction signals skin cells to produce more melanin as a protective response.
Do not stop wearing sunscreen just because you are staying indoors or working near windows; UVA rays and visible light penetrate window glass.
Do not expect overnight fixes. Melasma develops over months and takes sustained, gentle treatment over several months to fade.
medicationSafety: Triple combination creams (fluocinolone, hydroquinone, tretinoin) must be used strictly as directed by your dermatologist, typically for a few weeks only, and never as a daily fairness cream.
Hydroquinone should not be used continuously for prolonged periods without medical monitoring, as it can occasionally trigger paradoxical bluish-black deposits known as exogenous ochronosis.
If taking oral tranexamic acid, inform your doctor immediately if you have a personal or family history of deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, stroke, or heart disease.
Topical retinoids and hydroquinone must be discontinued during pregnancy and breastfeeding; always inform your doctor if you are planning to conceive.
Perform a small patch test behind your ear or along your jawline before introducing any new active serum or cream to check for allergic contact dermatitis.
complications: Significant emotional distress, anxiety, and lowered self-esteem due to appearance-related concerns.
Topical steroid-damaged facies (TSDF) from the misuse of steroid-containing fairness creams, presenting with skin thinning, visible spider veins (telangiectasia), pimples, and increased facial hair.
Exogenous ochronosis: A permanent, difficult-to-treat slate-grey or bluish-black pigmentation caused by excessive, unsupervised long-term hydroquinone use.
Post-inflammatory worsening: Rebound hyperpigmentation resulting from aggressive chemical peels, inappropriate laser settings, or harsh skin scrubbing.
emergencySigns: Rapidly growing, asymmetrical, multicoloured (black, brown, blue, or red) mole or dark patch with irregular borders: seek immediate medical evaluation to rule out melanoma or other skin malignancies.
Sudden burning, severe swelling, blistering, or oozing of the face following the application of any cream, peel, or home remedy.
Signs of systemic blood clots while taking prescribed oral tranexamic acid, such as sudden chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or painful swelling in one leg: call 108 or 112 immediately.
whenToSeeDoctor: You notice new, persistent dark patches on your face or body that do not fade with basic sun protection over several weeks.
Your pigmentation suddenly darkens, burns, or becomes intensely itchy.
You have been using an over-the-counter medical cream and notice facial hair growth, thinning skin, redness, or burning upon sun exposure.
You have dark, velvety skin around your neck or armpits accompanied by irregular menstrual periods or sudden weight gain.
You are pregnant, planning pregnancy, or taking hormones and notice rapid development of facial pigmentation.

faqs.q: Can melasma be cured permanently?
faqs.a: Melasma is a chronic condition, meaning it can be lightened significantly and kept well controlled, but no herb, diet or product can make it go away permanently. Sun exposure, heat, or hormonal changes can trigger a recurrence, which is why ongoing sun protection and maintenance skincare are essential.

faqs.q: Does drinking lots of water remove pigmentation?
faqs.a: Drinking adequate water supports general skin hydration and overall health, but water alone cannot dissolve or flush out excess melanin deposits in your skin layers. Targeted medical treatments and strict photoprotection are needed.

faqs.q: Are over-the-counter fairness creams safe for melasma?
faqs.a: Many creams sold across the counter in India contain powerful topical steroids or unregulated bleaching chemicals. While they may lighten the skin temporarily, they cause severe long-term complications including skin thinning, increased hair growth, and intense rebound darkening. Always use medicines prescribed by a qualified dermatologist.

faqs.q: Why does my melasma worsen in the summer or while cooking?
faqs.a: Melanocytes respond not only to ultraviolet rays but also to visible light and heat (infrared radiation). Cooking over hot stoves or walking in humid summer heat dilates blood vessels and stimulates pigment production. Tinted mineral sunscreens and proper ventilation help protect against this.

faqs.q: Can raw lemon juice or besan packs lighten my dark spots?
faqs.a: Lemon juice is highly acidic and frequently causes severe contact dermatitis, chemical burns, and deep post-inflammatory pigmentation on Indian skin. Besan (gram flour) is fine as a gentle wash, but aggressive rubbing will irritate the skin and darken patches further.

draft.definition: Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) refers to a predictable cluster of physical, emotional, and behavioural changes that occur during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle—the 7 to 14 days before a period starts—and resolve within a few days of bleeding. While mild premenstrual symptoms affect up to 75% to 80% of menstruating women at some point, Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD) is a much more severe, disabling form affecting approximately 3% to 8% of women. PMDD is recognized by medical bodies as an endocrine-related psychiatric condition characterized by profound mood changes, extreme irritability, anger, overwhelming fatigue, and depressive symptoms that significantly disrupt work, home, and personal relationships. Neither PMS nor PMDD is a character flaw, emotional weakness, or 'just in your head.' They are genuine neurobiological responses to the natural hormonal shifts of the menstrual cycle.

quickFacts.label: Timing
quickFacts.value: Occurs strictly during the luteal phase (1 to 2 weeks before menstruation starts)

quickFacts.label: Resolution
quickFacts.value: Symptoms subside within 4 to 7 days after the onset of menstrual bleeding

quickFacts.label: Mild to Moderate PMS
quickFacts.value: Experienced by roughly 75% of reproductive-age women

quickFacts.label: PMDD Prevalence
quickFacts.value: Affects about 3% to 8% of women (ACOG and DSM-5 criteria)

quickFacts.label: Primary Mechanism
quickFacts.value: Heightened brain sensitivity to normal shifts in estrogen and progesterone

quickFacts.label: Core PMDD Warning
quickFacts.value: Marked mood disruption, severe despair, or suicidal thoughts need urgent medical care

causes: Abnormal brain sensitivity to standard hormonal fluctuations: Estrogen and progesterone rise and fall normally during every ovulatory cycle, but individuals with PMS and PMDD have central nervous systems that are unusually sensitive to these shifts.

Serotonin dysregulation: Progesterone metabolites directly interact with gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and serotonin receptors in the brain. When hormone levels plummet prior to menstruation, serotonin signalling can fall sharply, triggering mood crashes, irritability, fatigue, and carbohydrate cravings.
Genetic factors: Twin and molecular studies show clear heritability for premenstrual mood disorders. Specific differences in cellular receptor genes alter how brain circuits respond to sex steroids.

Heightened stress and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis dysfunction: High ongoing psychological stress, unmanaged workplace strain, or past trauma can amplify brain reactivity to luteal-phase hormonal shifts.

Suboptimal nutrient intake: Diets lacking sufficient calcium, magnesium, B vitamins, and complex carbohydrates can impair neurotransmitter synthesis and worsen water retention and neuromuscular irritability.

Inflammatory pathways: Elevated levels of high-sensitivity C-reactive protein and other inflammatory cytokines during the luteal phase have been associated with increased abdominal bloating, fluid retention, breast tenderness, and mood disturbances.

types.name: Mild to Moderate PMS
types.desc: The most common form. Involves manageable physical symptoms like mild abdominal fullness, water retention, breast tenderness, and mild mood shifts that do not cause significant family or occupational impairment.

types.name: Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD)
types.desc: A severe, diagnostic clinical entity. Marked by disabling mood lability, intense anger, interpersonal conflict, hopelessness, anxiety, severe lethargy, and a feeling of being completely overwhelmed or out of control during the luteal phase.

types.name: Premenstrual Exacerbation (PME)
types.desc: The premenstrual worsening of an underlying, continuous medical or psychiatric disorder—such as major depression, generalized anxiety disorder, migraine, irritable bowel syndrome, or asthma—which does not fully clear after menses.

diagnosis: Prospective daily symptom charting: The gold standard for diagnosing PMS and PMDD requires tracking symptoms every single day for at least two consecutive menstrual cycles using a validated tool, such as the Daily Record of Severity of Problems (DRSP).
Verification of a symptom-free follicular phase: Symptoms must clearly vanish within the first few days after menstrual bleeding begins and remain completely absent until after ovulation.

DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for PMDD: Requires at least 5 symptoms present in the final week before menses, with at least one core mood symptom (marked mood swings, irritability or anger, depressed mood or feelings of hopelessness, or severe anxiety).

Clinical exclusion: A thorough medical evaluation is conducted to rule out primary depressive disorders, generalized anxiety, chronic fatigue syndrome, perimenopause, endometriosis, and thyroid dysfunction that could mimic PMS symptoms.

investigations.purpose: Charts daily mood and physical changes across two complete cycles to confirm luteal-phase timing
Rules out hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism, which commonly mimic premenstrual fatigue, mood swings, and cycle changes
Screens for iron deficiency anemia, which frequently drives premenstrual exhaustion, brain fog, and breathlessness
Evaluates stored iron levels even if overall hemoglobin appears borderline normal
Assesses vitamin D sufficiency, as low levels are associated with worse premenstrual mood symptoms and bone aches
Checks for B12 deficiency, which can exacerbate premenstrual neurological symptoms, mood dips, and extreme lethargy
Checks for metabolic disturbances and reactive blood sugar drops that worsen luteal irritability and sugar cravings

modernTreatment: First-line lifestyle optimization: Setting up structured sleep habits, regular moderate exercise, balanced low-sodium meals, and stress reduction methods form the clinical baseline for everyone.

Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT): Structured sessions with a clinical psychologist help develop effective coping strategies, challenge catastrophic thinking patterns, and reduce relational distress during symptomatic weeks.

Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs): Widely endorsed as the first-line pharmacotherapy for PMDD. Because the mechanism in PMDD works rapidly via neurosteroid receptor pathways, doctors may prescribe SSRIs either continuously every day or intermittently (taken only during the luteal phase, starting at ovulation and stopping at period onset).

Combined Oral Contraceptives: Formulations that suppress ovulation—especially those containing drospirenone with a shortened hormone-free interval—are clinically approved to stabilize hormonal swings in PMDD and moderate PMS.

Symptomatic pain relief: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or paracetamol may be used during symptomatic days to ease breast tenderness, headaches, joint pain, and uterine cramps as advised by your doctor.

Nutritional supplementation: Doctors often recommend evidence-supported supplements including calcium, magnesium, and vitamin B6 to support neurotransmitter balance and reduce premenstrual water retention.
ayurvedaView: In classical Ayurveda, premenstrual distress is understood through the disruption of Doshas, predominantly involving Apana Vata (the sub-dosha governing pelvic organs, downward movement, and elimination) and Pitta (governing metabolic transformations and blood/Rakta).
When Apana Vata is obstructed or vitiated by irregular routines, poor sleep, or dry foods, symptoms like abdominal distension, constipation, back pain, and anxiety emerge before menses.
When Pitta is aggravated by excessive spicy, sour, fried, or salty foods, symptoms lean toward irritability, anger, hot sensations, acne breakouts, and tender, swollen breasts.

Traditional texts describe the concept of Artava Pravritti (healthy menstrual flow), emphasizing gentle digestive fires (Agni), adequate hydration, calming daily rhythms (Dinacharya), and light, warm, unctuous meals.
Herbal remedies and Panchakarma modalities are viewed strictly as traditional supportive practices alongside modern medical care, never as standalone cures.

herbsUsed.name: Ginger
herbsUsed.note: Studied for its natural anti-inflammatory actions. Clinical trials suggest it may help ease premenstrual physical discomfort, cramps, nausea, and abdominal bloating when taken during the late luteal phase as advised by your doctor.

herbsUsed.name: Ashwagandha
herbsUsed.note: An established adaptogen evaluated for chronic stress and nervous exhaustion. It may support restful sleep, calm the nervous system, and help moderate premenstrual anxiety alongside standard medical advice.

herbsUsed.name: Shatavari
herbsUsed.note: Traditionally utilized in Ayurveda to nourish female reproductive health. Scientific human trials are limited, but it is traditionally used to support energy, soothe irritability, and promote vitality.

nutrition: Prioritize complex carbohydrates: Incorporate wholesome Indian grains such as jowar, bajra, ragi, brown rice, steel-cut oats, and whole wheat rotis. Complex carbs facilitate steady insulin release, which aids brain tryptophan uptake and helps maintain stable serotonin levels.

Sharply reduce hidden sodium: Avoid excessive table salt, pickles (achaar), papad, namkeen, packaged chips, bhujia, canned soups, and restaurant gravies during the two weeks before your period. High sodium worsens breast engorgement, peripheral edema, and abdominal tightness.

Boost dietary calcium and magnesium: Consume fresh curd (dahi), paneer, buttermilk, ragi, roasted sesame seeds (til), soaked almonds, and dark green leafy vegetables like palak, methi, and drumstick leaves to reduce neuromuscular irritability and mood dips.

Curtail caffeine and energy drinks: High caffeine intake amplifies breast tenderness (mastalgia), triggers jitteriness, increases resting heart rate, and fragments sleep during the sensitive luteal window.

Limit refined sugar and confectionery: Heavy intake of sweets, mithai, chocolates, and sweetened beverages causes rapid blood sugar spikes followed by steep crashes, making luteal mood swings, fatigue, and headaches significantly worse.
Hydrate with soothing fluids: Drink 2 to 3 litres of clean water daily, supplemented with tender coconut water, diluted chaas, or warm jeera water to aid renal fluid clearance and alleviate bloating.
lifestyle: Maintain a prospective cycle and mood log: Use a simple paper calendar or a reputable tracking app to mark your cycle days, physical symptoms, and mood shifts. Seeing the clear pattern brings predictability and peace of mind.

Keep a rigid, restorative sleep schedule: Strive for 7 to 9 hours of uninterrupted sleep every night. Hormonal shifts elevate baseline body temperature slightly in the luteal phase, which can disrupt deep sleep; keep your bedroom cool and dark.

Adopt regular aerobic activity: Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic exercise per week, such as brisk walking, cycling, swimming, or light dancing. Physical activity releases endorphins, lifts mood, and naturally mobilizes retained fluids.

Schedule proactive downtime during late luteal days: Whenever possible, avoid scheduling emotionally exhausting meetings, major family negotiations, or peak workloads during the 3 to 5 days right before your period is due.

Eliminate tobacco and strictly moderate alcohol: Both smoking and alcohol intake disrupt steroid hormone metabolism, impair liver clearance of estrogens, and aggravate premenstrual insomnia and depression.
yogaActivity: Restorative asanas: Practice calming postures such as Supta Baddha Konasana (Reclining Bound Angle Pose), Balasana (Child's Pose), and Viparita Karani (Legs-Up-The-Wall Pose) with cushions or bolsters to release pelvic tension and soothe the nervous system.
Gentle spinal mobility: Practice gentle Marjaryasana-Bitilasana (Cat-Cow Pose) and soft seated twists to relieve lower back achiness and premenstrual digestive sluggishness.

Pranayama for mental equilibrium: Incorporate 10 to 15 minutes of Anulom Vilom (alternate nostril breathing) and Bhramari (humming bee breath). These slow-breathing techniques activate parasympathetic tone and alleviate sudden waves of irritability.

Avoid strenuous exhaustion: During days with intense fatigue, severe cramps, or heavy premenstrual heaviness, avoid strenuous, heated vinyasa flows, advanced inversions, or rapid breath-holding practices (Kumbhaka).
homeopathyNote: Homeopathic preparations are frequently promoted for menstrual complaints, mood swings, and water retention.

Rigorous systematic reviews and clinical trial evaluations have found no consistent scientific evidence that homeopathic remedies treat or alter the biological course of PMS or PMDD beyond a placebo effect.

Individuals experiencing disabling mood symptoms, severe functional impairment, or self-harm thoughts should seek care from qualified gynecologists and mental health professionals rather than relying on unproven alternatives.
evidenceNotes: Strong evidence: Prospective daily symptom charting is necessary for an accurate diagnosis. Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs) have high-level randomized controlled trial evidence demonstrating substantial symptom reduction in PMDD. Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) provides proven, durable coping benefits.

Moderate evidence: Regular moderate aerobic exercise, reducing excess dietary sodium, and clinical supplementation with calcium (under medical guidance) show consistent benefit in reducing physical and emotional PMS symptom severity.

Limited or mixed evidence: Herbal extracts such as ginger, ashwagandha, and vitex agnus-castus have shown promising preliminary results in small trials, but require larger, standardized studies before they can be considered primary therapies.
No credible evidence: Quick-fix detox teas, hormonal balancing tonics, and over-the-counter PMDD cure packages sold online have no verified clinical efficacy.
shouldNotDo: Do not brush off severe emotional distress as ordinary moodiness or PMS: If you feel intense despair, rage, or self-loathing every month, it may be PMDD, which requires structured medical support.
Do not stop or adjust prescribed SSRIs or hormonal medications on your own: Abruptly stopping antidepressants can trigger withdrawal symptoms and a severe rebound of mood instability.

Do not binge on high-sodium snacks, fried foods, and sugary sweets during craving spikes: While cravings are chemically driven by low serotonin, indulging them creates an inflammatory cycle that deepens fatigue and bloating.
Do not rely solely on memory to describe your symptoms to your doctor: Retrospective recall is notoriously inaccurate; always bring two full months of prospective daily symptom logs.
Do not overuse over-the-counter painkillers: Taking excessive NSAIDs without a doctor's guidance can cause gastritis, gastric ulcers, and kidney strain.
medicationSafety: Follow your doctor's exact regimen for SSRIs: If prescribed intermittent luteal-phase dosing, start and stop strictly on the designated cycle days; do not alter dosages without consulting your physician.

Report side effects promptly: If an antidepressant causes dry mouth, mild nausea, insomnia, or changes in libido, inform your doctor; different agents or dosage adjustments can significantly improve comfort.

Combined hormonal contraceptives require medical screening: Oral contraceptive pills carry specific medical contraindications, including uncontrolled hypertension, active liver disease, migraine with aura, and elevated thrombosis risk. Never start birth control pills without a full clinical evaluation.
Ensure safe pain medication practices: When using medications like paracetamol for pain or body aches, stay within the maximum safe limits advised by your doctor to protect liver function.
complications: Severe disruption of marital, family, and social relationships due to recurrent, monthly episodes of intense irritability, anger, and withdrawal
Marked occupational disability, missed work days, reduced workplace productivity, and impaired career progression during symptomatic weeks
Increased risk of secondary major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety, and substance misuse used as an unhealthy coping mechanism
Risk of self-harm, suicidal ideation, and suicide attempts in severe, untreated PMDD cases
Chronic sleep disturbances leading to metabolic dysregulation, fatigue, and lower overall quality of life
emergencySigns: Active suicidal thoughts, impulses to harm yourself, or feelings that your family would be better off without you: Seek emergency medical care immediately or contact a mental health crisis lifeline (such as Tele-MANAS at 14416)
Sudden, uncontrollable impulses of physical violence or extreme rage toward family members or children
Severe, agonizing abdominal or pelvic pain that does not respond to prescribed analgesics, which may indicate an acute surgical issue such as ovarian torsion or ectopic pregnancy
Sudden shortness of breath, one-sided leg swelling, or chest pain if taking combined oral contraceptives, which may indicate a blood clot (deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism)
whenToSeeDoctor: Your premenstrual mood changes cause noticeable friction in your marriage, family life, or professional relationships
You regularly feel overwhelmed, hopeless, or unable to perform daily tasks during the 7 to 10 days before your period
Physical symptoms like headaches, severe bloating, or breast pain prevent you from exercising or carrying out normal routines
Your symptoms do not disappear after your menstrual period begins, suggesting an underlying depression or anxiety condition rather than pure PMS
You have tracked your symptoms on a daily calendar for two cycles and notice a distinct, recurring luteal pattern

faqs.q: How can I tell the difference between normal PMS and PMDD?
faqs.a: Normal PMS causes mild to moderate physical and emotional symptoms (such as mild bloating, breast tenderness, or occasional irritability) that do not stop you from living your everyday life. PMDD is far more severe, characterized by disabling mood symptoms like deep despair, intense rage, severe panic, hopelessness, and extreme fatigue that disrupt your ability to work, study, or maintain personal relationships.

faqs.q: Why do I get intense cravings for sweets and namkeen before my period?
faqs.a: During the late luteal phase, the drop in estrogen and altered progesterone metabolites can cause a brief drop in brain serotonin levels. Consuming carbohydrates temporarily boosts insulin, which helps the amino acid tryptophan enter the brain to produce serotonin. Stress-related cortisol spikes also stimulate appetite for salty and sugary comfort foods.

faqs.q: Can diet and exercise alone completely resolve PMDD?
faqs.a: For mild to moderate PMS, diet, regular exercise, and stress management are often very effective. However, for true PMDD, lifestyle changes are usually a supportive foundation rather than a complete solution. PMDD frequently requires medical treatments such as SSRIs or specific hormonal therapies alongside psychological support like CBT.

faqs.q: Why do some doctors prescribe antidepressants only for two weeks a month?
faqs.a: In PMDD, SSRIs work through a rapid neurosteroid mechanism on brain GABA-A receptors, rather than taking 4 to 6 weeks as they do in typical major depression. Because of this rapid response, doctors often prescribe them only during the luteal phase (from ovulation until bleeding starts), which provides symptom relief with fewer long-term side effects.

faqs.q: Does PMS get worse as women get older?
faqs.a: Premenstrual symptoms can intensify during perimenopause—typically in a woman's late 30s and 40s—because hormonal fluctuations become more erratic and unpredictable before ovulation stops entirely. Symptoms permanently resolve after menopause once menstrual cycles cease.
